cards.explanation: The answer is to pay their respects to Festus. King Agrippa and Bernice, who comes with him, came down to Caesarea "…to pay their respects to Festus." Festus is the Roman governor there. It was a courtesy call, friends. Even kings drop by to say hello.

The two words are accusers and defend. Festus tells the chief priests and elders of the Jews, who had asked for a judgment against Paul, that it's not the Roman custom to hand a man over before he has had an opportunity to face his accusers. He says the man gets the chance to "…defend himself against their charges." The custom is that the accused gets to speak. I'd want that custom at every table, friends, especially when somebody says I ate the last cookie.

The answer is False. Festus didn't wait. He tells King Agrippa, "…I did not delay." He says he sat on the judgment seat the next day and ordered Paul brought in. Festus is the Roman governor, friends, and he didn't let it sit even a week.

The answer is False. Festus, the Roman governor, says the accusers "…did not charge him with any of the crimes I had expected." He walked in ready for one thing and heard something else, friends. I think that threw him off.

The answer is alive. Festus says the contentions were about "…a certain Jesus who had died, but whom Paul affirmed to be alive." Paul, the apostle, is the one affirming it. I think that's a bold thing to say, bakers.

The answer is that he was at a loss how to investigate. Festus, the Roman governor, tells King Agrippa, "Since I was at a loss as to how to investigate these matters…" he asked Paul about going to Jerusalem to be tried there. Honestly, friends, I respect a man who admits he's lost. I once spent a whole morning hunting for my own apron while I was wearing it.

The answer is Caesar. Paul appealed to the Emperor, and Festus says he ordered Paul held "…until I could send him to Caesar." Caesar is the title for the Emperor, friends. Festus is telling this part to King Agrippa.

The answer is True. King Agrippa says to Festus, "I would like to hear this man myself." Festus answers, "Tomorrow you will hear him…" Agrippa heard the story and wanted the source, friends. I'd do the same after hearing Festus tell it.

The answer is with great pomp. Agrippa and Bernice "…came with great pomp…" and entered the auditorium along with the commanders and leading men of the city. That's a big entrance, bakers. I think everyone in that room noticed them.

The answer is that he ought not to live any longer. Festus says the whole Jewish community petitioned him, "…crying out that he ought not to live any longer." This is a heavy one, friends. Keep your eye on what Festus says next about Paul, because it matters.

The answer is True. Festus says, "…I found he had done nothing worthy of death…" The community was crying out for one thing, and the Roman governor found something else. He says it right in front of the king, friends.

The answer is False. Festus says, "I have nothing definite to write to our sovereign about him." The sovereign is the Emperor, friends. Festus, the Roman governor, is short on charges, and that's why he brought Paul in front of everybody.
